newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Tung's advisors deny conflict with civil servants.
newsitem.headline: Tung's advisors deny conflict with civil servants.

text.p: Advisors of Hong Kong's future leader Tung Chee-hwa denied on Thursday rumours of a rift between them and civil servants, saying they had no plans to change the way the territory is run after it reverts to China.

At a discussion panel to introduce themselves to the media, members of Tung's executive council said they would not usurp the traditional policy-making role of the civil service and the council would not become a "cabinet".
"The rumour is grossly exaggerated. The executive council will not be a cabinet," said executive councillor Raymond Chien.
Chien's comments come after widespread speculation in Hong Kong that Tung's advisors could play policy-making roles from July 1, when the British-run territory passes back to Chinese rule.

In Hong Kong's current executive-led administration, civil servants traditionally formulate and carry out policy. Legislators vote on laws and budgets drawn up by bureaucrats, but rarely initiate policies.
The rumours began after Tung appointed three members of his future council earlier in 1997 to set up taskforces to tackle problems affecting Hong Kong's housing, education and care of the elderly.

Another executive councillor Yang Ti Liang, who resigned as Hong Kong's Chief Justice last year to vie with Tung for the territory's future leadership, gave his own assurance that things would not change after July 1.
"We shall carry on very much as we do now," Yang said at the same meeting.
"I don't think we will embark on new changes," he said, adding that Hong Kong already had enough changes to adjust to after the handover.
